subject: science
prompt_en: Neha writes: 'A periscope bends light round corners with its tube.' Correct her.
prompt_hi: Neha likhti hai: 'Periscope apni tube se roshni ko mod deta hai.' Use sahi karo.
answer: The tube does not bend light; light travels in straight lines and is turned by reflection off two plane mirrors placed at 45°.

subject: science
prompt_en: Draw (or describe) a ray diagram for a pinhole camera viewing a candle-shaped cut-out lit from behind: show two rays from the top and bottom.
prompt_hi: Pinhole camera ke liye ray diagram banao (ya batao), peeche se roshan mombatti ke aakar ke cut-out ko dekhte hue: upar aur neeche se do kirne dikhaao.
answer: A straight ray from the top of the object passes through the pinhole to the bottom of the screen; a ray from the bottom passes through to the top; the image is inverted between them.

subject: science
prompt_en: A kaleidoscope uses three mirror strips at 60° to each other. Why do a few broken bangle pieces inside look like a big, repeating pattern?
prompt_hi: Kaleidoscope mein 3 sheeshe ki pattiyaan 60° pe lagi hoti hain. Andar tooti chooriyon ke kuch tukde bade, dohraate pattern jaise kyun dikhte hain?
answer: The bangle pieces are reflected again and again between the mirrors, making many images arranged symmetrically, which form the pattern; turning the tube rearranges the pieces and changes the pattern.

subject: science
prompt_en: Soldiers in trenches and sailors in submarines use periscopes. In a crowd at a cricket match, how could a simple periscope help you, and how would you hold it?
prompt_hi: Khandakon mein sainik aur pandubbi mein naavik periscope use karte hain. Cricket match ki bheed mein simple periscope tumhari kaise madad kar sakta hai, aur use kaise pakdoge?
answer: Hold it upright with the top opening above people's heads facing the field; light from the field reflects off the top mirror down to the bottom mirror and into your eye, so you can see over the crowd.

subject: science
prompt_en: Explain to a friend how to make a pinhole camera at home from a box and butter paper, and what they will see.
prompt_hi: Dost ko samjhao ghar pe dabbe aur butter paper se pinhole camera kaise banaayein, aur kya dikhega.
answer: Key ideas: a closed box (or two sliding tubes) with a tiny hole at one end and butter paper at the other; point at a bright object (not the Sun) and look at the screen in shade; the image is small and inverted because light travels straight; screen nearer gives a smaller image.

subject: science
prompt_en: From memory: what kind of image (upright or inverted) does a periscope give, and how many mirrors does it use?
prompt_hi: Yaad se batao: periscope kaisi image deta hai (seedhi ya ulti), aur kitne sheeshe use karta hai?
answer: An upright image, using two plane mirrors.

subject: science
prompt_en: In a dark room, shine a torch on a globe (or a ball with a dot marking India). Before you turn it, predict: if you spin the globe slowly from west to east, from which direction will the 'Sun' first appear for the dot?
prompt_hi: Andhere kamre mein globe (ya ball jispe India ka nishaan ho) pe torch daalo. Ghumaane se pehle guess karo: globe ko pashchim se poorab dheere ghumaane pe, nishaan ke liye 'Sooraj' kis disha se pehle dikhega?
answer: From the east: the dot turns into the light from the eastern side, which is why the Sun appears to rise in the east.

subject: science
prompt_en: Predict: does the Sun rise earlier in Itanagar (Arunachal Pradesh) or in Dwarka (Gujarat)? By roughly how much?
prompt_hi: Guess karo: Sooraj Itanagar (Arunachal Pradesh) mein pehle ugta hai ya Dwarka (Gujarat) mein? Lagbhag kitna pehle?
answer: Itanagar, roughly an hour and a half earlier (about 1 hour 40 minutes), because it lies about 25 degrees of longitude to the east and the Earth rotates from west to east, so it turns into sunlight first (about 4 minutes per degree).

subject: science
prompt_en: Why do we have a 29 February only once every four years?
prompt_hi: 29 February chaar saal mein sirf ek baar kyun aati hai?
answer: One revolution takes about 365¼ days; the extra quarter day each year adds up to one full day every four years, which is added as 29 February in a leap year.

subject: science
prompt_en: If the Earth is spinning so fast, why do we not feel it moving, and why does the Sun seem to move across the sky instead?
prompt_hi: Agar Earth itni tezi se ghoom rahi hai, toh hum use mehsoos kyun nahi karte, aur ulta Sooraj aasmaan mein chalta kyun dikhta hai?
answer: We move along with the Earth smoothly at a steady speed, so we do not feel it; from the moving Earth, the Sun appears to move from east to west, just as trees seem to move backwards from a smooth-running train.

subject: science
prompt_en: Compare rotation and revolution of the Earth: what each is, how long it takes, and what it gives us.
prompt_hi: Earth ke rotation aur revolution ki tulna karo: dono kya hain, kitna samay lete hain, aur humein kya dete hain.
answer: Rotation: spinning on its axis, about 24 hours, gives day and night. Revolution: moving around the Sun, about 365¼ days, gives the year.

subject: science
prompt_en: Ishaan says: 'At night the Sun goes under the Earth and comes back up in the morning.' What is wrong?
prompt_hi: Ishaan kehta hai: 'Raat ko Sooraj Earth ke neeche chala jaata hai aur subah wapas upar aata hai.' Kya galat hai?
answer: The Sun does not go around the Earth daily; the Earth rotates, so our side turns away from the Sun at night and back towards it in the morning.

subject: science
prompt_en: Draw (or describe) the Earth and Sun from above the North Pole. Mark the day side and night side, and an arrow for the Earth's spin.
prompt_hi: North Pole ke upar se Earth aur Sooraj banao (ya batao). Din wala hissa aur raat wala hissa, aur Earth ke ghoomne ka teer dikhaao.
answer: The half facing the Sun is day; the far half is night; seen from above the North Pole, the Earth spins anticlockwise (west to east).

subject: science
prompt_en: Your uncle in New York calls at 8 pm Indian time and says he is having breakfast. Explain how this can be.
prompt_hi: Tumhare chacha New York se Indian time raat 8 baje phone karte hain aur kehte hain ki woh nashta kar rahe hain. Ye kaise ho sakta hai?
answer: New York is on the other side of the Earth; when India has turned away from the Sun (evening/night), New York is turning into sunlight (morning), because the Earth rotates.

subject: science
prompt_en: Ancient Indian astronomer Aryabhata wrote that the stars seem to move west because the Earth spins, like stationary objects on the bank seem to move backward to a person in a moving boat. Explain his comparison.
prompt_hi: Prachin bhaarteeya khagolshaastri Aryabhata ne likha ki taare pashchim ki or chalte dikhte hain kyunki Earth ghoomti hai, jaise chalti naav mein baithe insaan ko kinaare ki sthir cheezein peeche jaati dikhti hain. Unki tulna samjhao.
answer: In a moving boat, the still trees on the bank appear to move the opposite way; similarly, as the Earth spins from west to east, the still stars appear to move from east to west.

subject: science
prompt_en: Explain to your younger cousin, using a ball and a torch, why we have day and night and why the Sun rises in the east.
prompt_hi: Chhote cousin ko ball aur torch se samjhao ki din aur raat kyun hote hain aur Sooraj poorab mein kyun ugta hai.
answer: Key ideas: the Earth is a ball lit by the Sun on one half; it spins on its axis from west to east in about 24 hours; the lit half has day, the other night; turning eastward into the light makes the Sun appear to rise in the east.

subject: science
prompt_en: From memory: how long does the Earth take to go once around the Sun?
prompt_hi: Yaad se batao: Earth ko Sooraj ka ek chakkar lagaane mein kitna samay lagta hai?
answer: About 365¼ days (one year).

subject: science
prompt_en: Shine a torch straight down on squared paper and count roughly how many squares are lit. Then tilt the torch at a slant from the same height. Before you do, predict: will the lit patch get bigger or smaller, brighter or dimmer?
prompt_hi: Torch ko squared paper pe seedha neeche chamkaao aur lagbhag gino kitne khaane roshan hain. Phir usi oonchaai se torch ko tircha karo. Karne se pehle guess karo: roshan hissa bada hoga ya chhota, chamakdaar ya dhundhla?
answer: Bigger and dimmer: the same light spreads over more squares, so each square gets less light and heat, like slanting winter sunlight.

subject: science
prompt_en: In June it is summer in Delhi. Predict the season in Sydney, Australia, at the same time, and explain.
prompt_hi: June mein Delhi mein garmi hoti hai. Usi samay Sydney, Australia mein kaunsa mausam hoga, guess karo aur samjhao.
answer: Winter, because in June the southern hemisphere is tilted away from the Sun, getting slanting rays and shorter days.

subject: science
prompt_en: Why are days longer than nights in Delhi in June?
prompt_hi: June mein Delhi mein din raaton se lambe kyun hote hain?
answer: In June the northern hemisphere is tilted towards the Sun, so places like Delhi spend more of each rotation in the lit half, giving longer days.

subject: science
prompt_en: Compare summer and winter in India: the angle of the Sun's rays at noon and the length of the day.
prompt_hi: India mein garmi aur sardi ki tulna karo: dopahar mein Sooraj ki kirnon ka kon aur din ki lambaai.
answer: Summer: the noon Sun is high, rays fall more directly, days are longer. Winter: the noon Sun is lower, rays slant and spread out, days are shorter.

subject: science
prompt_en: A website says: 'We have summer because the Earth moves closer to the Sun.' Give two pieces of evidence that this is wrong.
prompt_hi: Ek website kehti hai: 'Garmi isliye hoti hai kyunki Earth Sooraj ke paas aa jaati hai.' Do saboot do ki ye galat hai.
answer: 1) The Earth is closest to the Sun in early January, during northern winter. 2) The two hemispheres have opposite seasons at the same time, which distance cannot explain since both are at the same distance.

subject: science
prompt_en: Draw (or describe) the Earth at two places in its orbit, June and December, with the tilted axis. Show which hemisphere is tilted towards the Sun in each.
prompt_hi: Orbit mein do jagah Earth banao (ya batao), June aur December, jhuki axis ke saath. Dikhaao har ek mein kaunsa hemisphere Sooraj ki taraf jhuka hai.
answer: June: the axis tilts the North Pole towards the Sun, so the northern hemisphere is tilted towards it. December (opposite side of the orbit): the axis still points the same way, so now the South Pole side is towards the Sun.

subject: science
prompt_en: Near the equator, in places like Singapore, there is little difference between summer and winter. Using the tilt idea, suggest why.
prompt_hi: Bhoomadhya rekha ke paas, jaise Singapore mein, garmi aur sardi mein zyada farak nahi hota. Tilt ke idea se kaaran socho.
answer: Near the equator the Sun is high in the sky all year and day length stays close to 12 hours, so the heating changes little through the year.

subject: science
prompt_en: Indian Antarctic stations Maitri and Bharati see the Sun not setting for weeks in December-January. Explain using the tilt.
prompt_hi: Bhaarat ke Antarctic station Maitri aur Bharati par December-January mein hafton tak Sooraj nahi doobta. Tilt se samjhao.
answer: In December-January the southern hemisphere is tilted towards the Sun, so the region near the South Pole stays in the lit half throughout each rotation, giving continuous daylight.

subject: science
prompt_en: Explain to a friend, with a ball and a torch, why India has summer in May-June and winter in December-January.
prompt_hi: Ek dost ko ball aur torch se samjhao ki India mein May-June mein garmi aur December-January mein sardi kyun hoti hai.
answer: Key ideas: Earth's axis is tilted and keeps pointing the same way; in May-June the north is tilted towards the Sun, giving direct rays and long days; in December-January it is tilted away, giving slanting rays and short days; distance is not the reason.

subject: science
prompt_en: From memory: in which month is the Earth closest to the Sun?
prompt_hi: Yaad se batao: Earth kis mahine mein Sooraj ke sabse paas hoti hai?
answer: Early January.

subject: science
prompt_en: In a dark room, put a torch (Sun), a small ball (Moon) and a big ball (Earth) in a straight line with the small ball in the middle. Before you look, predict what falls on the big ball.
prompt_hi: Andhere kamre mein torch (Sooraj), chhoti ball (Chaand) aur badi ball (Earth) ek seedhi line mein rakho, chhoti ball beech mein. Dekhne se pehle guess karo badi ball pe kya padega.
answer: The small ball's shadow falls on a small part of the big ball: this models a solar eclipse, seen only from the places where the Moon's shadow falls.

subject: science
prompt_en: Now place the big ball (Earth) in the middle, between the torch and the small ball. Predict what happens to the small ball, and which eclipse this is.
prompt_hi: Ab badi ball (Earth) ko beech mein rakho, torch aur chhoti ball ke beech. Guess karo chhoti ball ka kya hoga, aur ye kaunsa grahan hai.
answer: The small ball goes into the big ball's shadow and becomes dark: this models a lunar eclipse.

subject: science
prompt_en: With one lamp in a room, hold a ball on a stick at arm's length and slowly turn around on the spot. Predict how much of the lit part of the ball you will see when it is between you and the lamp, and when the lamp is behind you.
prompt_hi: Kamre mein ek lamp ho, ek ball ko danda pe haath bhar door pakdo aur dheere-dheere apni jagah ghoomo. Guess karo ball ka roshan hissa kitna dikhega jab ball tumhare aur lamp ke beech ho, aur jab lamp tumhare peeche ho.
answer: Between you and the lamp: almost none (like a new moon). Lamp behind you (ball held up so your head's shadow does not fall on it): the whole lit face (like a full moon). In between you see partly lit shapes, which are the phases.

subject: science
prompt_en: On which day can a lunar eclipse happen?
prompt_hi: Chandra grahan kis din ho sakta hai?
answer: Full moon (purnima).

subject: science
prompt_en: Why does an eclipse not happen every month?
prompt_hi: Har mahine grahan kyun nahi hota?
answer: The Moon's orbit is tilted by about 5° to the Earth's orbit, so in most months the Moon passes a little above or below the line joining the Sun and Earth, and no shadow falls exactly.

subject: science
prompt_en: Compare a half moon and a partial lunar eclipse: what causes the dark part in each?
prompt_hi: Aadhe chaand aur aanshik chandra grahan ki tulna karo: dono mein kaala hissa kis wajah se hai?
answer: Half moon: we are seeing half of the Moon's sunlit side; the dark part is the Moon's own night side. Partial lunar eclipse: the Earth's shadow is falling on part of the Moon.

subject: science
prompt_en: A friend says: 'During a solar eclipse the Sun is covered, so I can look at it with my sunglasses.' Explain why this is dangerous and give a safe method.
prompt_hi: Ek dost kehta hai: 'Surya grahan mein Sooraj dhak jaata hai, toh main sunglasses se dekh sakta hoon.' Samjhao ye khatarnaak kyun hai aur surakshit tareeka batao.
answer: Even the uncovered part of the Sun is bright enough to damage the eyes permanently, and sunglasses do not block enough; use pinhole projection onto paper (looking at the paper, not the Sun) or certified eclipse glasses.

subject: science
prompt_en: Draw (or describe) the positions of the Sun, Earth and Moon during a solar eclipse and during a lunar eclipse.
prompt_hi: Surya grahan aur chandra grahan ke samay Sooraj, Earth aur Chaand ki sthiti banao (ya batao).
answer: Solar eclipse: Sun, Moon, Earth in a line (Moon in the middle). Lunar eclipse: Sun, Earth, Moon in a line (Earth in the middle).

subject: science
prompt_en: During a total lunar eclipse the Moon often looks a dull coppery red rather than completely black. Is the Moon making its own light now? What is the more likely reason?
prompt_hi: Poore chandra grahan mein Chaand aksar bilkul kaala nahi balki halka taambe jaisa laal dikhta hai. Kya Chaand ab khud roshni de raha hai? Zyada sambhav kaaran kya hai?
answer: No, the Moon is still non-luminous; a little sunlight is bent through the Earth's atmosphere into the shadow, and mostly reddish light gets through (like the red of sunsets), dimly lighting the Moon.

subject: science
prompt_en: Your school plans to watch a partial solar eclipse. Using only a sheet of cardboard and a white paper, describe a safe way for everyone to watch it.
prompt_hi: Tumhaara school aanshik surya grahan dekhna chahta hai. Sirf ek gatte aur safed kaagaz se sabke liye surakshit tareeka batao.
answer: Make a small hole in the cardboard; stand with your back to the Sun; let sunlight pass through the hole onto the white paper held a little away; look only at the paper, where a small image of the partly covered Sun appears. Never look at the Sun through the hole.

subject: science
prompt_en: Explain to your family the difference between a solar eclipse, a lunar eclipse and the phases of the Moon.
prompt_hi: Apne parivaar ko surya grahan, chandra grahan aur chaand ki kalaaon ka farak samjhao.
answer: Key ideas: solar eclipse, Moon between Sun and Earth, Moon's shadow on Earth, at new moon, never look directly; lunar eclipse, Earth between Sun and Moon, Earth's shadow on Moon, at full moon, safe to view; phases, how much of the Moon's sunlit half we see, every month, not a shadow; eclipses are rare because the Moon's orbit is tilted.

subject: science
prompt_en: From memory: is it safe to watch a lunar eclipse with your naked eyes?
prompt_hi: Yaad se batao: kya chandra grahan nangi aankhon se dekhna surakshit hai?
answer: Yes, a lunar eclipse is safe to watch with the naked eye, because we are looking at the Moon, not the Sun.

subject: sst
prompt_en: You take a train from Delhi to Chennai. Using a physical map, describe in words which kinds of land you would pass through.
prompt_hi: Tum Delhi se Chennai train se jaa rahe ho. Physical map dekh ke shabdon mein batao ki raaste mein kaun-kaun si zameen aayegi.
answer: Flat Northern Plains around Delhi, then hilly central highlands, then the Peninsular (Deccan) Plateau, and finally the low Eastern Coastal Plain near Chennai.
